claims.text: Rapid melt-spinning at 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbon.
The proposed intervention is a short sub-Tx flash anneal immediately after rapid quenching, monitored by fast DSC.
The flash anneal should be performed at approximately 850 K for 0.5–2 seconds.
Approximately 850 K is just below the primary crystallization onset of this alloy.
A brief sub-Tx anneal causes atomic-scale relaxation and homogenization of the amorphous matrix.
The flash anneal reduces heterogeneous nucleation sites in the amorphous alloy.
The brief anneal relieves internal stresses without crossing the nucleation threshold.
Controlled structural relaxation increases the kinetic barrier to crystallization.
The increased crystallization barrier prevents or suppresses primary non-eutectic phase formation during subsequent slower reheating.
Without flash annealing, melt-spun ribbons crystallize through a multistep process during slower reheating.
Slow cooling produces a complex multiphase crystalline microstructure, whereas faster cooling reduces the number of crystalline phases.
Flash-annealed samples will retain a more stable amorphous structure than unannealed melt-spun samples.
Flash annealing will suppress and delay the exothermic crystallization peak during subsequent DSC reheating.
Flash annealing will improve thermal stability under repeated thermal cycles.
The melt-spinning cooling rate must remain within 10^5–10^6 K/s to obtain the intended amorphous starting state.
The useful flash-annealing window is narrowly bounded near 850 K and 0.5–2 seconds.
Minor deviations from the proposed annealing temperature or duration may trigger unwanted nucleation.
Earlier DSC exotherms or increased XRD/TEM crystallinity in flash-annealed samples relative to unannealed controls would falsify the predicted benefit.
